title: Coordinate-Free Summaries
notes: Open by naming the central discipline of the chapter: do not average angle labels when the object is a direction. The source span covers printed pages 13 through 24 and PDF pages 32 through 42, but this deck follows the executable notebook route: turn directions into unit vectors, summarize geometry, then check invariance.

title: The Chapter Route
notes: Use the route map to frame every statistic as a choice of loss or moment on the circle. The mean direction comes from a vector resultant, dispersion asks how costly a candidate direction is, the median swaps chord loss for arc loss, moments fold the circle, and grouping needs a correction.

title: Why Angle Labels Betray The Sample
notes: This slide should make the coordinate error vivid. The same cluster sits across the zero cut, so the ordinary average near 160.7 degrees is mostly a bookkeeping artifact. Moving the cut opposite the cluster gives about 0.7 degrees, while the circular resultant points there without asking for a cut.

title: Resultant Vector As Center Of Mass
notes: Present the resultant as an average in the plane, not as an average of degrees. The coordinates C and S are mean cosine and mean sine. When the resultant is nonzero, atan2 returns the mean direction and the length Rbar measures how strongly the sample agrees.

title: Rotation Equivariance Is The Test
notes: The invariance check is the proof habit students should keep. Rotating every observation by a fixed delta rotates the mean direction by that delta and preserves Rbar. The sine residual around the mean vanishes, which is the circular analogue of a first-order balance condition.

title: Resultant Length Measures Concentration
notes: Explain concentration with cancellation. Samples pointing together have a long average vector; samples spread around the circle cancel toward the origin. The statistic V equals one minus Rbar, so low variance means the resultant nearly reaches the boundary of the unit disk.

title: Dispersion Is A Loss Landscape
notes: Use the graph as a loss landscape rather than a black-box formula. Chord dispersion is minimized at the mean direction, and the notebook verifies the identity D(alpha) equals V plus a penalty depending only on the angular gap from the mean. That identity is why the mean is geometrically natural.

title: Circular Median Uses Arc Loss
notes: Separate robustness from concentration. The circular median minimizes average shortest-arc distance, so one observation on the opposite side can pull the vector mean while leaving the median near the dense cluster. The median is a location summary under an L1 geometry on the circle.

title: Trigonometric Moments Fold The Circle
notes: Introduce trigonometric moments as repeated wrapping before averaging. The first moment is the resultant; the second moment doubles angles so opposing directions can agree. Moment length records strength, while the phase records the axis or direction after undoing the fold.

title: Moment Diagnostics Beyond Location
notes: Use the mini table to connect the visual to reproducible numbers from the notebook. R1 is about 0.800, R2 about 0.385, and the centered second moment carries skewness and kurtosis information. The key message is that higher moments summarize shape, not just location.

title: Grouped Data Shortens Resultants
notes: Grouping is a measurement operation, not merely a storage format. Replacing every observation in a bin by the midpoint compresses within-bin angular variation, so resultant lengths tend to be biased downward as the bins become coarse. Equal-width grouping lets the bias be approximately undone.

title: The Correction Factor Is Local
notes: The correction factor should be read as a small-angle expansion. For small h it is nearly one, which explains why fine grouping barely changes the answer. At forty-five degrees the factor is about 1.026, large enough to matter but still not a cure for every circular data problem.

title: Two Mistakes, Two Remedies
notes: Draw a firm distinction between the two failure modes. Grouping correction repairs a known loss of concentration caused by midpoint bins. It does not legitimize a linear mean that depends on an arbitrary cut point; the coordinate-free representation is still the first line of defense.

title: Notebook Checks As Invariants
notes: This slide turns the notebook checks into lecture evidence. Rotation equivariance, a zero sine residual, the chord-dispersion identity, moment centering, and the grouping series are not optional tests; they are the invariant scaffolds that show the summaries are circular rather than linear.

title: Operational Checklist
notes: Close with an operational checklist students can apply to any small circular sample. Embed angles as unit complex numbers, read the resultant, choose a loss for dispersion or median behavior, inspect higher moments for folded structure, and correct grouping only when the binning assumptions are actually present.
